senses.gloss: A man whose job is to repair and maintain machines or appliances.
examples: The furnace quit overnight, so a *serviceman* came out first thing.
Two *servicemen* from the cable company spent an hour on the roof.
The *serviceman* said the compressor was shot and the fridge wasn't worth fixing.

senses.gloss: A place where a group of people have come to live, especially a small or newly founded one.
examples: The first *settlement* here was a trading post on the river.
Archaeologists found three ancient *settlements* under the field.
A few families started a *settlement* at the edge of the desert.

senses.gloss: The act of cutting something off or breaking off a connection completely.
examples: The *severance* of diplomatic ties came after months of warnings.
His *severance* from the family business was sudden and bitter.
The vote led to a complete *severance* of trade between the two countries.

senses.gloss: The act or process of sending goods somewhere.
examples: The order is packed and ready for *shipment*.
*Shipment* of the vaccine began the week after approval.
Delays in *shipment* cost the company its biggest customer.

senses.gloss: A route that is shorter or quicker than the usual one.
examples: We took a *shortcut* through the parking lot.
There's no *shortcut* to the lake; you have to follow the road around.
He knows every *shortcut* in the city and still got us there late.

senses.gloss: A quicker way of doing something that skips the usual steps, often at some cost.
examples: There are no *shortcuts* to learning an instrument.
The contractor took *shortcuts*, and the deck fell apart in two years.
She wanted a *shortcut*, but the paperwork had to be done properly.

senses.gloss: The strip of ground or pavement along the edge of a road, where a vehicle can pull over.
examples: He pulled onto the *shoulder* and put on his hazard lights.
A deer was standing on the *shoulder* of the highway.
The *shoulder* is soft here, so don't park off the pavement.

senses.gloss: A cut of meat from the upper front leg of an animal.
examples: She braised a pork *shoulder* all afternoon.
Lamb *shoulder* is cheaper than the leg and just as good.
Ask the butcher for a five-pound *shoulder*.

senses.gloss: A glass case in a store or museum in which things are displayed.
examples: The bakery's *showcase* was full of pies.
The rings are locked in the *showcase* by the register.
Someone smashed one of the *showcases* and took two watches.

senses.gloss: The loss of a store's goods to theft, damage, or bookkeeping errors.
examples: *Shrinkage* ate up almost two percent of the chain's sales.
Cameras at the exits cut *shrinkage* in half.
Store managers get a bonus if *shrinkage* stays under target.

senses.gloss: The stopping of a machine, plant, or system, either for repairs or for good.
examples: The refinery is in a two-week *shutdown* for maintenance.
A safety sensor triggered an emergency *shutdown* of the reactor.
The plant *shutdown* put three hundred people out of work.

senses.gloss: A business or activity that someone does in addition to their main job.
examples: He teaches history and repairs guitars as a *sideline*.
What started as a *sideline* now brings in more than her salary.
The farm has a couple of *sidelines*, like selling hay and boarding horses.

senses.gloss: A distinctive feature or pattern by which something can be recognized.
examples: The satellite picks up the heat *signature* of a running engine.
That chord change is a *signature* of his early records.
Investigators matched the chemical *signature* of the two samples.

senses.gloss: The supporting frame of a building, ship, or other structure.
examples: The steel *skeleton* of the tower went up in four months.
Only the *skeleton* of the old barn is still standing.
Welders put the *skeleton* of the hull together in the yard.

senses.gloss: The bare outline or essential structure of a plan, story, or argument.
examples: He has the *skeleton* of a novel and not much else.
We agreed on the *skeleton* of the deal and left the details to the lawyers.
Start with a *skeleton* of the essay, then fill in the examples.

senses.gloss: An insulting word for someone thought to be too easily offended or too fragile.
examples: He calls anyone who disagrees with him a *snowflake*.
The column dismissed the protesting students as *snowflakes*.
Don't be such a *snowflake* — it was a joke.

senses.gloss: An easy question asked to let someone look good, especially in an interview.
examples: The host lobbed him one *softball* after another.
Reporters were promised a real interview and got nothing but *softballs*.
That wasn't a tough question; it was a *softball*.

senses.gloss: A single gem, usually a diamond, set by itself in a ring or other piece of jewelry.
examples: He proposed with a half-carat *solitaire*.
She wears a plain gold band and a *solitaire*.
The case held a row of diamond *solitaires*.

senses.gloss: A way of dealing with a problem, or the answer to a puzzle or question.
examples: Nobody at the meeting had a *solution* to the parking problem.
The *solution* to the puzzle is printed on the last page.
Cheaper housing is only part of the *solution*.

senses.gloss: The particular branch of work or study that someone concentrates on.
examples: Her *specialty* is pediatric surgery.
Tax law is not my *specialty*.
The clinic has doctors in six different *specialties*.

senses.gloss: Eyeglasses, in the plural form spectacles.
examples: He polished his *spectacles* with the end of his tie.
A pair of wire-rimmed *spectacles* sat on the desk.
She peered over her *spectacles* at the class.

senses.gloss: The buying of property, stocks, or goods in the hope of selling them later at a profit.
examples: Land *speculation* pushed prices out of reach for local families.
The crash was blamed on years of reckless *speculation*.
He made and lost a fortune on currency *speculation*.
